title: Meta creates stock with no vote to pay for AI
statLabel: Meta's free cash flow, Q3 2026, after $34.9B of capital spending in the quarter
body: Meta's board approved a new Class C share that carries no voting rights, to be handed to every shareholder as a one-share-for-one dividend once a charter change takes effect on January 19, 2027. Meta says the new class is for raising capital, paying employees and funding acquisitions, and that the dividend will not change anyone's voting power. The timing follows a quarter in which revenue rose 26% to $64.6 billion but spending on data centers and chips reached $34.9 billion, pushing free cash flow below zero. Alphabet took the same route in 2014 and this year issued $85 billion of new stock for AI, half of it without votes, according to Semafor.
why: When a company sells shares to raise money, existing owners get diluted, and nonvoting shares let founders raise that money without giving up control. If you own big tech through an index fund, you are buying more economic ownership with less say over how it is spent. The questions to watch are how many new shares get sold, and whether the AI spending earns more than the capital it costs.

sources.name: Meta Platforms, Q3 2026 results press release (SEC Exhibit 99.1), Oct 21, 2026

title: Traders now put an 88% chance on another Fed hike in December
statLabel: Probability of a December 2026 Fed rate hike priced by fed funds futures, CME FedWatch, Oct 21, 2026
body: The Federal Reserve already raised its target range by a quarter point to 3.75%-4.00% on September 16, and September consumer prices rose 3.7% from a year earlier, above forecasts. With Brent crude back above $110 a barrel this week, futures traders see only about a 15% chance of another hike at the October 27-28 meeting but an 88% chance by December, according to CME's FedWatch tool, and nearly all economists in a Reuters poll expect the same skip-then-hike path. Those odds are not a survey: they are worked out from the prices of 30-day fed funds futures, which trade at 100 minus the average rate the market expects for a month. Gold, which pays no interest, slipped for a fourth straight session to about $4,119 an ounce as hike bets held.
why: Expected Fed moves get built into prices long before the meeting, so mortgage rates, savings yields and bond prices are already moving on that 88%. If you are choosing between locking a CD, a mortgage rate or a bond fund's duration, the question is not what the Fed will do but whether it will do more or less than is already priced. A surprise in either direction is what moves markets on the day.

sources.name: Admirals, Central bank super week, Oct 21, 2026

title: Homebuilders are the gloomiest since 2012, and 43% are cutting prices
statLabel: NAHB/Wells Fargo builder confidence index, October 2026, lowest since June 2012 (50 is neutral)
body: The National Association of Home Builders' confidence index fell three points to 29 in October, its lowest reading since June 2012. Prospective buyer traffic dropped five points to 18, the weakest since April 2012 apart from the pandemic shock of April 2020. To keep homes selling, 43% of builders cut prices, the highest share since at least 2020, with an average cut of 6%, and 65% offered other incentives such as paying to lower buyers' mortgage rates. The trigger is borrowing costs: Freddie Mac's average 30-year mortgage rate was 7.40% last week, the highest in nearly three years, while energy, diesel and construction-loan costs squeeze builders' margins.
why: When builders are discounting, the sticker price is not the real price: incentives such as a paid-down mortgage rate can be worth more than a price cut, and they are negotiable. For anyone who owns builder stocks or works near housing, falling buyer traffic is an early warning for orders, jobs and spending on furniture and appliances. For owners locked into a low mortgage rate, it explains why new homes, not resales, are where prices are giving way first.

title: MSCI writes new rules that could drop bitcoin-holding companies
statLabel: Share of Strategy's basic shares held by funds tracking MSCI's global indexes, per the company, Oct 2026
body: On October 15, MSCI, one of the largest index providers, finalized rules for companies that mostly hold investments rather than run a business. Instead of its earlier test, which flagged firms whose digital assets were at least 50% of total assets, MSCI will now screen operating assets and five financial ratios, starting with its November index review. A current member is removed only if it fails the screen in both of its two most recent annual filings, and MSCI will publish the list of companies at risk on November 11. Strategy, the largest public bitcoin holder, says index funds tracking MSCI hold about 13 million of its shares, about 3.1% of its basic shares, and its shares fell about 3% before the market opened the next day.
why: If you own an index fund, a committee's rulebook decides which companies you own, not you and not a stock picker. A rule change can force billions of dollars of automatic buying or selling regardless of a company's prospects. Knowing how your fund's index is built tells you what you actually hold and why it changes.

title: Lenders charge France far more than Germany, before a ratings test
statLabel: Extra yield on France's 10-year bond over Germany's, Oct 16, 2026 · Ideal Investisseur
body: On October 16, France's 10-year government bond yielded 4.79% against 3.42% for Germany's, a gap of 137 basis points. In early September the gap was about 85, and on October 2 it hit 147, its widest since the euro debt crisis, briefly making France costlier to fund than Italy or Greece. Almost all of the jump came from French yields rising, not German ones falling. The causes are a deficit near 5.4% of GDP, against an EU limit of 3%, debt near 120% of GDP, and a parliament with no stable majority. A first budget vote is due October 20, and Moody's, which rates France Aa3 with a negative outlook, reviews it on October 23.
why: A country's bond yield is the floor under borrowing costs for its banks, companies and mortgages, so a rising spread spreads. France's interest bill could top €91 billion by 2027, close to 3% of GDP, money that cannot go to anything else. If you own European bonds, European bank shares or a global bond fund, check how much France and other high-debt euro countries make up, because that is where this risk would show up.

title: Goldman's stock-trading revenue jumps 72% as markets churn
statLabel: Rise in Goldman Sachs equities revenue, Q3 2026 vs a year earlier · Goldman 8-K, Oct 2026
body: Goldman Sachs earned $6.44 billion from equities in the third quarter, up 72% from a year earlier, and more than half of it, $3.37 billion, came from financing: lending to hedge funds and other big traders so they can hold larger positions. That financing line alone rose 96%. Bond and currency trading went the other way, slipping 1% at Goldman and about 4% at JPMorgan, whose equities revenue still rose about 49% to roughly $5 billion. Underneath the trading noise, ordinary lending held steady: JPMorgan's net interest income rose 12.8% to about $27 billion and Citigroup's rose 13.7% to about $17 billion, while Wells Fargo set aside $1.03 billion for bad loans, up from $681 million a year earlier.
why: A trading boom is a reading on how much risk and borrowed money is sloshing through markets, and the fastest-growing piece here is loans to professional traders. Revenue that depends on volatility and leverage can shrink as fast as it grew, which is why investors usually pay less for a dollar of trading profit than for a dollar of steady fees or loan income. When you read any company's results, ask which part of the growth repeats every quarter and which part depends on the weather in markets.

title: Lenders now charge an AI cloud company 15% to borrow
statLabel: Yield on CoreWeave's 9.625% bonds due 2032 · Benzinga, Oct 15, 2026
body: CoreWeave rents Nvidia chips to AI companies and has paid for its data centers largely with debt: about $35.6 billion of principal outstanding at the end of June. Its $1.25 billion of 9.625% bonds due 2032, sold only in June, fell to about 78 cents on the dollar this week, which pushed their yield above 15%; S&P rates the company B+, which is junk. The stock dropped about 16% on October 14 to $65.78, and the scare spread to Oracle, another heavy borrower for AI capacity, which fell nearly 9%. The pressure shows in the accounts: in the second quarter CoreWeave's net interest expense was $640 million, up 140% and nearly a quarter of its $2.58 billion revenue.
why: Demand for AI is not the question the bond market is asking; the question is whether the returns on borrowed money will beat what that money costs. When a company's cost of capital jumps, growth that looked profitable at 9% can destroy value at 15%, and shareholders sit behind lenders in line. If you own broad index funds, AI-linked companies are a large share of them, so watch interest bills and refinancing, not just revenue headlines.

title: Europe's gas price hits a four-year high before winter
statLabel: Dutch TTF gas, Europe's benchmark, four-year high · CaixaBank Research, Oct 14, 2026
body: Europe's benchmark natural gas price, Dutch TTF, reached €85.9 per megawatt-hour on October 14, its highest in four years, and Trading Economics puts it roughly 160% above a year ago. The squeeze comes from the Strait of Hormuz: Qatar's LNG must sail through it, no Qatari cargoes are reaching Europe, and Persian Gulf supply is about 20% of world LNG exports. Storage is the second problem. EU tanks were about 74% full on October 14, against a 15-year average near 90% for this point in the season, so Europe has to keep bidding against Asia for spot cargoes just as heating demand starts.
why: Gas sets the price of a large share of Europe's electricity and feeds fertilizer, chemicals and glass, so a gas spike shows up in power bills, food prices and factory margins months later. Gas also has no single world price: US buyers pay a regional price that follows different forces, so watch where the companies you own or buy from actually source their energy.

title: Gasoline pushes US inflation to 3.7%
statLabel: US consumer prices, 12 months to September 2026 · BLS, Oct 14, 2026
body: Consumer prices rose 0.6% in September and 3.7% over the past year, up from 3.4% in August. Gasoline jumped 9.1% in the month and 34.2% over the year, and the Bureau of Labor Statistics says it accounted for over half of the monthly increase. Core inflation, which leaves out food and energy, rose 0.3% in the month and 2.6% over the year, a bit above the 2.5% economists expected, with shelter, airfares and used cars doing the pushing. The 10-year Treasury yield rose to about 5.28% that morning as investors weighed whether the Fed raises rates again at its October 28 meeting.
why: Headline inflation tells you what your budget feels; core tells you what is likely to stick. Energy shocks can reverse, but if core keeps creeping up, borrowing costs stay high for longer, which matters for mortgages, business loans and the real return on cash. Check whether your savings rate is beating 3.7% before taxes.

sources.name: US Bureau of Labor Statistics, CPI release, Oct 14, 2026

title: A Chinese chip claim knocks 10% off SK hynix in a day
statLabel: SK hynix share price change on Oct 13, 2026, Korea JoongAng Daily
body: Over the weekend, the president of ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT), China's largest DRAM maker, said it plans to ship DDR5 server memory built on a new '4F²' cell design by the end of 2026. That layout packs memory cells into roughly 30% less space than today's mainstream design, which could make each bit cheaper to produce. Memory stocks fell on Monday, with Micron down about 4%, and on Tuesday in Seoul SK hynix closed down 10.09% and Samsung Electronics down 7.39%, while the Kospi briefly dropped below 6,000 and triggered a trading curb. Morningstar analysts said mass-producing the design reliably will be 'extremely difficult', and the shortage is still in place: TrendForce expects conventional DRAM contract prices to rise another 10–15% this quarter.
why: Memory chips are close to a commodity, so the biggest risk to today's record profits is new supply, not falling demand. Micron's adjusted gross margin hit 87% last quarter, up from 45.7% a year earlier, and markets now react sharply to any sign that a competitor could add capacity. If you own broad Korea, chip or AI funds, check how much of them sits in just three memory makers.

title: Oil tops $106 again, and diesel is the real squeeze
statLabel: US average diesel price per gallon, AAA · Oct 9, 2026
body: Brent crude rose to about $106 a barrel on Monday after Houthi strikes on Riyadh's international airport killed 12 people and two tankers were attacked near Oman and in the Strait of Hormuz, a route that carried about a fifth of global oil and LNG trade before the Iran war. Diesel is under even more pressure than crude: the US average is $6.28 a gallon, near the record $6.52 set on September 22, and the US diesel crack spread (diesel price minus crude price) passed $100 a barrel for the first time in August. Russian diesel output is down about 30% after Ukrainian strikes on its refineries, and US refineries ran at 98% of capacity in late August, the most since 2018. On October 9 the White House announced a deal for Russian diesel, starting with more than 300,000 tons, but analysts quoted by AP expect little effect on prices.
why: Diesel moves trucks, tractors, ships and generators, so its price shows up later in groceries, delivery fees and anything that has to be shipped. If your business moves goods, check whether your carriers add fuel surcharges and how fast they pass them on. Wednesday's September inflation report will show how much of this is already reaching consumer prices.

title: Long-term rates are above 5%, and mortgages followed
body: The Fed's target rate is 3.75–4.00% after a hike in September, with the effective rate at 3.88%. But the 10-year Treasury yield, which long-term loans follow, has climbed to 5.22%, and 30-year fixed mortgages average about 7.5%. Households now expect 3.9% inflation over the next year, the highest since May 2023, so lenders want more yield to lock money up for a decade.
why: Borrowing for a home or a business costs more, for longer. Cash and short-term Treasuries pay well right now, while long bonds swing with every inflation report. Watch the September inflation report on October 14 and the Fed decision on October 28.
